messages.content: I want to build an incremental Java taint analyzer. The central requirement is to preserve interprocedural soundness when method-body edits change heap aliasing or virtual dispatch.

That sets a demanding correctness target for an incremental analysis. A method-body edit may affect more than the edited method: a changed alias relationship can alter how taint moves through heap objects, and a changed virtual call can alter which method bodies contribute to a result. The incremental analyzer must account for those effects across method boundaries rather than treating the edited body as an isolated unit.
What exactly is the correctness comparison?

For Java without reflection or native calls, the incremental analyzer’s findings must equal those of a sound, context-sensitive whole-program recomputation. Equality matters here: it is not enough merely to retain some notion of soundness while producing a different set of findings. For each relevant edited program, the incremental result is compared with what that whole-program analysis would find.
So the restriction to Java without reflection or native calls is part of the requirement, not just an example?

Yes. It defines the stated scope of the findings-equality requirement. The goal does not specify what should happen for programs using reflection or native calls, so it would be unwarranted to extend this particular guarantee to them.
Can you explain why heap aliasing makes an edit difficult for an incremental taint analyzer?

Conceptually, two references may point to the same heap object. If an edit changes which references may alias, a write through one reference may newly matter—or cease to matter—to a read through another. That difference can affect taint propagation even when the read and write occur in different methods. An incremental result that overlooks the changed relationship could disagree with whole-program recomputation.
And virtual dispatch creates a similar cross-method concern?

Yes, although the mechanism is different. A virtual call’s possible targets determine which method behavior the analysis must consider. If an edit changes the relevant dispatch possibilities, taint effects associated with a call may change beyond the edited method. The goal requires the incremental findings to reflect such changes wherever they affect the context-sensitive whole-program result.
Does interprocedural soundness mean I can just revisit the edited method and its immediate callers?

The goal does not authorize a fixed stopping point such as immediate callers. The question is whether all effects needed to match the whole-program findings have been accounted for. An edit involving aliasing or dispatch can have consequences through multiple calls or heap accesses; the required result is defined by equality with recomputation, not by a particular boundary around the edit.
I also want the analyzer to be faster. State that part precisely.

The performance target is a median speedup of at least 3× over full recomputation on a fixed suite of 100 method-body edits. That is a comparative target for the specified suite, not a claim that every individual edit must achieve a 3× speedup.
Does the speed target relax the findings requirement for difficult edits?

No. Both requirements apply: findings must equal sound, context-sensitive whole-program recomputation for Java without reflection or native calls, and performance must reach at least a 3× median speedup over full recomputation on the fixed suite of 100 method-body edits. A fast update that misses a finding would not satisfy the correctness requirement.
When you say findings must equal recomputation, do you mean only that the incremental analyzer cannot omit findings?

The stated requirement is stronger than a no-omissions condition. It says the findings must equal those of the specified whole-program recomputation. That rules out both missing findings and additional findings relative to that comparison result, even though sound analyses in general may differ in precision.
How should I think about context sensitivity in that comparison?

It means the reference is a context-sensitive whole-program analysis, rather than an unspecified context-insensitive one. The node does not prescribe a particular way of representing contexts. What it does require is that the incremental analyzer reproduce the findings of the sound, context-sensitive recomputation being used for comparison.
Could an edit affect the result even if its text says nothing explicitly about taint?

In principle, yes. An edit can change aliasing or possible virtual-call targets, which can in turn change how taint moves through the program. The relevant question is not whether the edit visibly mentions taint, but whether its effects alter the findings that whole-program recomputation would produce.
I don't want to accidentally describe a particular incremental algorithm as already chosen. What can be said without doing that?

You can state the required behavior without committing to an implementation: after a method-body edit, account for any consequences of changed heap aliasing and virtual dispatch that matter to interprocedural taint findings; for the stated Java scope, return exactly the findings of sound, context-sensitive whole-program recomputation; and meet the specified median speedup target on the fixed edit suite. That describes outcomes, not a chosen update mechanism.
Is the 100-edit suite itself specified in any more detail?

No further composition is given. It is specified as a fixed suite of 100 method-body edits, with full recomputation as the speed comparison. Nothing here identifies the particular programs, edits, timing procedure, or observed measurements.
Then I should not present the speedup as an achieved result yet?
Correct. “Achieve ≥3× median speedup” states a target. The supplied goal does not report a completed measurement or say that the threshold has already been reached.
Give me one concise formulation that keeps the difficult cases and both acceptance criteria visible.

Build an incremental Java taint analyzer that preserves interprocedural soundness when method-body edits change heap aliasing or virtual dispatch. For Java without reflection or native calls, its findings must equal those of sound, context-sensitive whole-program recomputation, while achieving at least a 3× median speedup over full recomputation on a fixed suite of 100 method-body edits.

To pursue that goal, I propose maintaining provenance-indexed, context-sensitive heap points-to facts, virtual-call targets, and taint facts, then retracting and recomputing affected dependency SCCs after an edit.

That is an incremental-analysis proposal rather than a reported result. It connects the three kinds of information implicated by the goal: heap points-to facts describe possible aliasing, virtual-call targets describe possible dispatch, and taint facts describe the findings-relevant flow. Provenance and dependencies are intended to identify which of those facts may need reconsideration after a method-body edit.
What does “provenance-indexed” contribute here?

At a conceptual level, provenance records where an analysis fact’s support comes from, so an edit can be related to facts that may depend on the changed program content. Indexing that information makes it possible to look up potentially affected facts rather than assuming that every stored fact is unaffected or recomputing everything by default. The proposal does not specify a particular provenance representation.
Why maintain provenance for points-to and call targets as well as taint facts? Aren’t taint findings the output I care about?

They are the output being compared, but changes upstream can alter them. A changed heap points-to fact can change which accesses may refer to the same object; a changed virtual-call target can change which method behavior a call may involve. If the incremental analysis tracks provenance only for existing taint facts, it may not have enough information to identify all taint consequences of those changed relationships. The proposal therefore includes provenance-indexed information for all three categories.
And “context-sensitive” applies to those maintained facts, not just to the final taint result?

Yes. The proposal describes context-sensitive heap points-to, virtual-call-target, and taint facts. The exact form of context sensitivity is not specified here. The important point is that incremental maintenance must preserve the distinctions relevant to matching the sound, context-sensitive whole-program recomputation named in the goal.
Can you unpack the dependency SCC part without assuming a particular implementation?

SCC stands for strongly connected component. In a dependency graph, facts or computations can depend on one another in a cycle; an SCC groups the mutually reachable parts of that graph. “Retract and recompute affected dependency SCCs” proposes reconsidering the cyclic dependency regions affected by an edit, rather than treating each potentially invalidated fact as independent. It does not, by itself, specify the graph’s exact node granularity or the mechanics of recomputation.
Why might retraction matter instead of merely adding newly derived facts?

A method-body edit can remove a basis for an existing points-to relationship, virtual-call target, or taint fact, as well as introduce new possibilities. An additions-only update would not address facts whose support has disappeared. Retraction is the part of the proposal that acknowledges those disappearing supports; recomputation addresses what remains or arises in the affected dependency regions.
Does retraction mean deleting every fact linked to the edited method?

Not necessarily. A fact could have support independent of the edited content. Provenance is relevant precisely because the analysis needs to distinguish a support that changed from one that still holds. The proposal says to retract and recompute affected dependency SCCs; it does not say that all facts associated with an edited method must be permanently deleted.
Suppose changing aliasing affects a possible call target, which then affects taint. Is that the sort of dependency this proposal is meant to capture?

Yes, as a general illustration of why the three fact categories need to be considered together. If an edit changes a relevant points-to relationship, consequences may extend to virtual dispatch and then to taint. The proposal’s dependency-based treatment is meant to make such interprocedural effects eligible for reconsideration, including when dependencies form cycles. That illustration is not a claim about a particular program or observed edit.
Is recomputing affected SCCs the same thing as recomputing the whole program?

Not by definition. The proposal focuses recomputation on dependency SCCs identified as affected. Depending on the dependencies for a given edit, the affected portion could be smaller or larger. The proposal does not guarantee that every edit will require only a small update, nor does it supply a measured speedup.
Could I call this approach sound just because it tracks provenance and SCCs?

Those features alone do not establish soundness or equality of findings. The proposal would have to account for all edit-induced effects relevant to heap aliasing, virtual dispatch, and taint across contexts and method boundaries. The correctness criterion remains equality with sound, context-sensitive whole-program recomputation for Java without reflection or native calls; this node proposes a way to pursue it, not a demonstration that it holds.
And the performance requirement is still the same comparison?

Yes. The target remains at least a 3× median speedup over full recomputation on the fixed suite of 100 method-body edits. Maintaining provenance and recomputing affected dependency SCCs is a proposed means of pursuing incremental efficiency, not evidence that the target has been achieved.
How would you phrase the proposal without smuggling in a detailed algorithm or a success claim?

Maintain provenance-indexed, context-sensitive heap points-to facts, virtual-call targets, and taint facts. After a method-body edit, retract and recompute affected dependency SCCs so that changes to aliasing or dispatch can be reflected in interprocedural taint analysis. This states the proposed approach without specifying an unprovided implementation or claiming that the correctness and speed targets have already been met.
Here’s the hard question for that proposal: how can newly introduced aliases and virtual targets trigger complete taint updates without recomputing unaffected contexts?

The difficulty is that a newly possible relationship may have no existing taint fact whose provenance points to it. An update cannot rely only on tracing the support of facts it already holds. Conceptually, it must also notice newly possible points-to relationships and call targets, determine which taint computations they can now influence, and follow those consequences across method boundaries. Avoiding recomputation in other contexts requires a defensible way to establish that those contexts cannot be influenced.
So provenance for existing taint facts is not enough to discover a new flow?

Right. Provenance can help explain why an existing fact holds and what might need retraction if its support changes. But if an alias or call target was previously absent, the taint consequence may also have been absent. The question is how to make the newly introduced relationship itself a trigger for reconsideration, rather than waiting for a taint fact that does not yet exist.
What does “complete” mean in this question? Does it mean rerunning everything?

No. It means not overlooking any taint change that follows from the new aliases or virtual targets. The challenge is to reach all affected facts and contexts while leaving genuinely unaffected contexts alone. Completeness of the update concerns the resulting findings; it does not prescribe whole-program recomputation as the update procedure.
Could the analyzer stop once it has handled the method whose body changed?

Not on that basis alone. A new alias can affect a heap access elsewhere, and a new virtual target can bring another method’s behavior into consideration. Any resulting taint change may propagate further. The stopping condition would have to depend on whether additional relevant consequences remain, not merely on whether the edited method has been revisited.
But if you follow every possible consequence, what keeps the update from expanding into every context?

That is the selectivity side of the open question. Context sensitivity provides distinctions between contexts, but the updater still needs to determine which of those distinctions matter to the changed relationships. It should not assume that every context is affected, or that a context is unaffected simply because it contains no currently recorded taint consequence of the new relationship. The proposal identifies provenance and dependency SCCs as relevant tools, but does not yet specify a rule that establishes that boundary.
Can you give a general illustration without assuming a particular implementation?

Imagine an edit makes two references potentially alias when the analysis previously did not relate them. A tainted write through one reference could now matter to a read through the other, and that read might occur through a different method context. The update has to discover the newly relevant read and any consequences flowing from it. It need not revisit an unrelated context merely because that context exists; the unresolved issue is how to justify that it is unrelated.
How does the same issue appear with virtual dispatch?

If a call gains a possible virtual target, the newly considered method behavior may contribute taint effects that were not present at that call before. Those effects could influence subsequent analysis in the calling context and beyond it. As with a new alias, looking only at previously recorded taint dependencies could miss the newly available path; the change in possible target must itself prompt examination of its consequences.
Does ‘affected dependency SCCs’ settle which contexts must be recomputed?

Not by itself. Recomputing affected SCCs describes what to do once the affected dependency region is known. Your question also asks how newly introduced relationships make that region discoverable, including dependencies that had no prior taint fact. It further asks how to avoid pulling in contexts that have no relevant dependency. The proposal leaves those boundary questions to be worked out.
Would it be fair to say that both additions and removals matter, but this question emphasizes additions?

Yes. The proposal includes retraction and recomputation, which speaks to changes in existing support as well as resulting updates. This question focuses on newly introduced aliases and virtual targets because they can create paths that were not represented among existing taint facts. Handling removals does not, by itself, answer how those new paths are discovered.
If a newly introduced target affects another context only indirectly, does ‘complete’ still cover that context?

Yes. If the target’s effects can propagate through dependencies into that context and change a taint finding, a complete update has to account for it. ‘Unaffected contexts’ means contexts whose relevant results do not depend on the change, not merely contexts that are several steps away from the edited method.
Can I claim that provenance indexing solves discovery of all newly introduced paths?

Not from what has been stated. Provenance indexing is part of the proposal, but its mere presence does not show that paths created by new alias or dispatch possibilities will be discovered. That is exactly what the question probes: how changes in those underlying facts become triggers for all relevant taint updates while recomputation remains confined to affected contexts.
What should an answer to this question ultimately make clear?

It should explain both sides of the boundary: why every taint consequence of a newly introduced alias or virtual target will be reconsidered, including indirect interprocedural consequences, and why contexts left untouched cannot acquire a different relevant result from that change. Without both, the proposed incremental update has not yet explained how it can be complete and selective at the same time.
My hypothesis is that provenance-indexed alias and dispatch edges, together with affected-SCC closure, should let us match recomputed findings while revisiting under 40% of facts.

That is a testable hypothesis, not an established outcome. It has two parts: the updated taint findings should match recomputed findings, and the update should revisit fewer than 40% of facts. The proposed connection is that provenance-indexed alias and dispatch edges make relevant changes discoverable, while affected-SCC closure carries their consequences through the dependency structure.
How does that address the question about newly introduced aliases and virtual targets?

It treats alias and dispatch edges as things whose changes can initiate an update, rather than relying only on provenance attached to existing taint facts. A newly introduced edge could therefore prompt examination of taint consequences that did not previously exist. Taking the affected-SCC closure is intended to follow dependencies beyond the first fact or context touched. The hypothesis is that this reaches the complete affected region without revisiting contexts outside it.
Are you saying it definitely reaches every new taint consequence?

No. “Should match recomputed findings” expresses the prediction. To establish it, the affected-SCC closure would have to include every dependency through which a new alias or virtual target can change a finding. The hypothesis does not itself prove that the recorded edges and dependencies are sufficient.
What does provenance add to an alias or dispatch edge specifically?

Conceptually, it relates the edge to the support from which the analysis derived it. That gives an incremental update a way to identify edges whose status may change after an edit. In this hypothesis, indexing those edges also matters because an added or changed relationship must be able to trigger downstream reconsideration; it cannot be treated solely as background information for existing taint facts. No particular provenance representation is specified.
And what is meant by ‘affected-SCC closure’ here?

It means considering not just an initially affected dependency SCC, but the SCCs reachable through relevant dependencies from it. That is the proposed way to carry an alias or dispatch change through cycles and onward to potentially changed taint results. The hypothesis does not specify the precise graph or a rule for identifying the initial affected SCCs.
Why mention closure instead of just the first SCC touched by the edit?

Because the edit’s effect need not stop at its first dependency region. A changed alias or virtual target can affect another computation, whose result can affect still another. Closure expresses the need to follow those consequences until there are no further affected dependency regions. Whether that process both catches every relevant region and excludes unrelated ones remains part of what the hypothesis predicts.
Does matching recomputed findings mean the results can merely be close?

No. Matching means equality of findings with recomputation, not approximate agreement or just retaining most findings. In the stated goal, the comparison is sound, context-sensitive whole-program recomputation for Java without reflection or native calls. The hypothesis predicts that the selective update can preserve that result.
What exactly does ‘under 40%’ say?

It says the update should revisit fewer than 40% of facts. It is a strict threshold: revisiting exactly 40% would not be under 40%. The hypothesis does not define a more detailed counting procedure or report an observed fraction, so it should not be presented as a measured result.
Is that the same as the speed target?

No. The under-40% figure concerns the fraction of facts revisited. The separate goal is at least a 3× median speedup over full recomputation on a fixed suite of 100 method-body edits. Reconsidering fewer facts could be relevant to performance, but the fact fraction alone does not establish an elapsed-time speedup.
Could matching findings still require visiting more facts than the hypothesis predicts?

Yes. The correctness and selectivity predictions are distinct. An update might match recomputation yet revisit 40% or more of facts; that would fail the under-40% part of this hypothesis. Conversely, revisiting under 40% would not be enough if the resulting findings differed from recomputation.
What if the new alias affects a context that has no existing taint fact connected to the edit?

That is precisely the discovery problem the hypothesis aims to address. The newly introduced alias edge, rather than an existing taint fact, would need to lead into the relevant dependency closure. If the dependency structure does not expose that connection, an affected-SCC update could leave that context untouched and fail to match recomputation. The hypothesis predicts that the proposed indexing and closure will avoid that gap; it does not demonstrate it.
Does the same reasoning apply to a newly possible virtual target?

Yes. The changed dispatch edge would need to trigger reconsideration of any taint consequences associated with the newly possible target, including consequences in other affected contexts. Closure is intended to carry those effects along relevant dependencies. It would be premature to claim that it does so completely without checking the resulting findings against recomputation.
Am I committing to recomputing every SCC reachable in the entire program?

The hypothesis says ‘affected-SCC closure,’ not an indiscriminate closure over every program SCC. Its selectivity claim depends on distinguishing relevant dependencies from unrelated regions. It does not yet specify the exact criterion for that distinction, so it should not be paraphrased as either whole-program SCC recomputation or a guaranteed minimal update.
Can we state the hypothesis in a way that keeps its uncertainty explicit?

Yes: provenance-indexed alias and dispatch edges with affected-SCC closure should allow incremental taint updates to match recomputed findings while revisiting under 40% of facts. ‘Should’ marks both the findings match and the fact-revisit bound as predictions to be evaluated, not results already achieved.
Let’s make the next step a plan: track provenance-backed alias and dispatch deltas, recompute transitive dependent context-sensitive SCCs, and validate findings and speedup on 100 edits.

That plan connects change detection, update scope, and evaluation. The alias and dispatch deltas identify relationships that changed after a method-body edit. Recomputing transitive dependent context-sensitive SCCs is intended to carry their consequences through the analysis without automatically revisiting unrelated contexts. Validation then compares the resulting findings and performance with full recomputation on the 100 edits. These are planned steps, not completed results.
What counts as an alias or dispatch delta in that wording?

A delta is a change in the analysis’s alias or virtual-dispatch relationships: a relationship may become possible or cease to be possible after the edit. Tracking both directions matters because a new relationship can introduce a taint path, while a lost relationship can remove support for one. The plan does not prescribe a particular representation for those changes.
Why call the deltas provenance-backed?

Provenance connects a derived relationship to its support, which helps the update relate a method-body change to alias or dispatch relationships that may need reconsideration. In the plan, the deltas are not merely a list of changed-looking results; they are tied to the analysis information used to identify and account for those changes. The exact provenance mechanism remains unspecified.
The earlier question was especially about newly introduced relationships. How does this plan speak to those?

It makes changes in alias and dispatch relationships explicit update triggers. A newly introduced alias or virtual target need not wait for an existing taint fact to point to it: its delta can initiate reconsideration of dependent analysis regions. Recomputing transitive dependents is then intended to reach taint consequences beyond the first affected region. Whether the tracked dependencies actually capture every such consequence is something the findings validation must check.
Why are the dependent SCCs transitive rather than just directly dependent?

An alias or dispatch change may affect one analysis result, which affects another, and so on across method boundaries. Restricting the update to direct dependents could stop before a changed taint finding is reached. ‘Transitive dependent’ expresses the plan to follow relevant dependency chains beyond that first step, including through strongly connected components where dependencies are cyclic.
And why say context-sensitive SCCs?

The update has to respect the context distinctions relevant to the context-sensitive analysis being compared against. Saying ‘context-sensitive SCCs’ keeps those distinctions in view when identifying and recomputing dependent regions. It does not specify how contexts are represented or how the SCC graph is constructed.
Is the plan to recompute every context that contains a call to the edited method?

The plan is to recompute transitive dependent context-sensitive SCCs, not to use a blanket rule based only on the presence of a call. A context might be affected through aliasing or dispatch without fitting that simple description, while another might not have a relevant dependency. The difficult part is identifying the dependency closure accurately enough to include the former and leave the latter alone.
Could ‘transitive’ accidentally imply recomputing the whole program after every edit?

No. It describes how far to follow dependencies from the changes, not an instruction to include every SCC regardless of dependency. For a particular edit, the affected closure could be broad; the plan does not promise a small closure every time. Its intended selectivity comes from limiting recomputation to regions that are dependent on the tracked deltas.
What happens in the plan when an edit removes an alias or possible virtual target?

That is also a delta to track. It can undermine the support for existing downstream facts, so the dependent regions need reconsideration rather than merely receiving additions. The plan says to recompute the transitive dependent SCCs; it does not specify the detailed retraction procedure or assume that every downstream fact necessarily disappears.
Could an unchanged taint fact still be inside a region that gets recomputed?

Yes. Recomputing an affected region does not imply that every result in it will change. The point is to determine which results remain supported after the alias or dispatch delta and which differ. The plan is selective about regions to reconsider, not a promise that every revisited fact will have a different value.
What exactly should findings validation compare?

It should compare the incremental taint findings with the findings from sound, context-sensitive whole-program recomputation for the stated scope: Java without reflection or native calls. The goal calls for equality of findings, so checking only that no findings were missed—or only that most findings agree—would not establish that criterion.
Does checking the 100 edits prove that equality for all programs in that scope?

No. Validation on the 100 edits can provide evidence for the plan on that fixed suite, but it is not by itself a universal proof for every Java program without reflection or native calls. The stated correctness requirement remains broader than any finite set of observations.
How should speedup be validated under this plan?

The comparison is with full recomputation on the fixed suite of 100 method-body edits. The goal is at least a 3× median speedup over that baseline. The plan calls for validating speedup; it does not report timings or establish that the median threshold has been reached.
Would a fast update with findings that differ from recomputation count as success?

No. Findings equality and speedup are separate requirements. Speed on the 100 edits would not excuse an incomplete or different set of findings. Equally, matching findings alone would not demonstrate the specified median speedup.
Is measuring how many facts were revisited part of this particular plan?

This plan explicitly calls for tracking provenance-backed alias and dispatch deltas, recomputing transitive dependent context-sensitive SCCs, and validating findings and speedup on 100 edits. It does not specify a fact-revisit measurement or a fact-revisit threshold, so those should not be presented as required results of this plan.
Can you restate the sequence without making it sound as if we have already implemented it?

The proposed sequence is to track provenance-backed changes in alias and virtual-dispatch relationships after method-body edits, use those changes to identify and recompute transitive dependent context-sensitive SCCs, and then validate incremental findings and speedup against full recomputation on the 100 edits. This describes what is to be done and checked, not what has already been observed.
For the evaluation activity, run AliasDispatch-100 method-body edits against context-sensitive whole-program recomputation. Measure finding equality, median speedup, and the revisited-fact fraction.

That specifies the comparison and the three measurements without reporting an outcome. AliasDispatch-100 is the named set of 100 method-body edits. The activity compares incremental analysis with context-sensitive whole-program recomputation, checking whether findings are equal, how their runtimes compare at the median, and what fraction of facts the incremental analysis revisits.
What does ‘finding equality’ require us to look for?

It requires comparing the findings produced after an edit with the findings from whole-program recomputation for that edited program. Equality means the sets agree, rather than merely having a substantial overlap or showing that the incremental analysis found no fewer results. This measurement bears directly on the stated correctness goal for Java without reflection or native calls.
Could a single unmatched finding be hidden by the speedup number?

No. Finding equality and median speedup are separate measurements. A speedup figure cannot turn unequal findings into equal ones. Conversely, equality alone would say nothing about whether the performance target was met.
Why explicitly say ‘context-sensitive whole-program recomputation’ in the activity?

It identifies the findings and runtime comparison baseline. Comparing against a different analysis could yield an agreement or speedup number that does not address the stated goal. The activity does not specify a particular representation of contexts; it specifies the kind of recomputation against which the incremental results are measured.
Does ‘run AliasDispatch-100’ tell us which kinds of edits are in it?

Not beyond what is stated: it is a named set of 100 method-body edits. The name should be preserved, but it does not by itself establish the programs involved, the distribution of edit types, or any measured behavior.
What is the median speedup meant to summarize?

It summarizes speed relative to full recomputation across the fixed set of 100 method-body edits. The goal’s threshold is at least a 3× median speedup over full recomputation; this activity measures the quantity needed to assess that target. It does not say that the measured median has reached 3×, and it does not require every individual edit to reach that value.
If one edit takes longer incrementally than full recomputation, does that alone settle the median result?

No. A median is a summary across the suite, so one edit’s comparison does not determine it. That edit would still contribute to the evaluation, but the activity provides no timings from which to calculate the median.
Why record a revisited-fact fraction in addition to speedup?

It measures how much analysis state the incremental update revisits, which is a different question from elapsed-time speed. It is also the measurement relevant to the hypothesis that the approach should revisit under 40% of facts while matching recomputed findings. The activity calls for measuring the fraction; it does not report a value or establish the hypothesis.
Does revisiting under 40% of facts automatically give a 3× median speedup?

No. The fraction of facts revisited and runtime speedup are distinct measurements. A smaller revisited fraction does not, by itself, determine the runtime comparison. Both are being measured rather than inferred from one another.
Is the denominator of the revisited-fact fraction specified precisely here?

No. The activity names the revisited-fact fraction but does not define a detailed counting convention or aggregation rule. We can say that the evaluation must measure that fraction; we should not invent a precise denominator or present an unreported percentage as an observation.
Can the activity tell us whether newly introduced aliases and virtual targets are handled completely?

Finding equality on the edits would test whether their incremental findings agree with whole-program recomputation. That is relevant to the concern about newly introduced aliases and virtual targets, but the activity statement contains no results, and observations on 100 edits alone would not constitute a universal proof for every program in the stated Java scope.
Should I describe AliasDispatch-100 as having already passed the comparison?

No. ‘Run AliasDispatch-100’ states the evaluation activity, not its outcome. Nothing in this node gives finding comparisons, runtimes, or revisited-fact measurements, so neither a pass nor a failure can be reported.
Then give me a precise description of the activity that keeps all three measurements visible.

Run the AliasDispatch-100 set of 100 method-body edits against context-sensitive whole-program recomputation. For the incremental analysis, measure equality of findings with recomputation, median speedup over full recomputation, and the fraction of facts revisited. Report the measurements as measurements when available, without assuming any outcome in advance.
The AliasDispatch-100 results are in: all 100 method-body edits matched whole-program findings. Median speedup was 3.7×, and 28% of facts were revisited.

Those are the three observed results for AliasDispatch-100: finding equality with whole-program recomputation on all 100 edits, a 3.7× median speedup over full recomputation, and a revisited-fact fraction of 28%. They describe this evaluation, rather than a result for every possible Java edit.
When I say all 100 edits matched, what exactly matched?

The incremental taint findings matched the findings from context-sensitive whole-program recomputation for each of the 100 method-body edits in AliasDispatch-100. That is a finding-level comparison, not merely a report that both analyses ran or that their outputs were similar.
Is it accurate to say there were no finding mismatches in the suite?
Yes. “All 100 edits matched whole-program findings” means no finding mismatch was reported for those 100 comparisons. It does not specify the number of individual findings in any edit.
Does the 3.7× figure mean every edit was 3.7 times faster?
No. It is the median speedup across AliasDispatch-100, not a speedup assigned to every individual edit. The evidence gives no per-edit speedups, so it cannot tell us how uniform performance was.
What baseline does that speedup use?
Full recomputation is the baseline. The 3.7× figure summarizes the measured incremental speedup relative to recomputing the analysis for the edits in AliasDispatch-100.
Should I translate 28% of facts revisited into a statement about runtime?

Keep them separate. The 28% figure reports the revisited-fact fraction; 3.7× reports median speedup. The evidence provides both measurements, but it does not establish that revisiting that fraction alone accounts for the measured runtime.
Does ‘28% revisited’ mean the other facts were proved unaffected?

Not from that measurement alone. It tells us the reported fraction of facts revisited, but it does not describe a proof about every fact that was not revisited. The findings comparison separately reports that the incremental and whole-program findings agreed on all 100 edits.
Can I describe 28% as the fraction on each edit?

No. The evidence reports “28% of facts revisited” for AliasDispatch-100 without a per-edit breakdown or a detailed aggregation convention. Presenting 28% as the value for each of the 100 edits would add information that was not reported.
Do the results tell us which edit produced the largest update?
No. They give an all-edits finding comparison, a median speedup, and a revisited-fact fraction. They do not identify any particular edit’s runtime or number of revisited facts.

I want to consider a proposal for the incremental Java taint analyzer: use differential Datalog with delete/rederive to maintain context-sensitive points-to, virtual-call, and taint relations incrementally from edited method facts.

The proposal treats facts from method bodies as inputs to related analysis relations. When a method body changes, its input facts change; differential Datalog would propagate the resulting changes through context-sensitive points-to, virtual-call, and taint relations. This is a proposed approach, not a claim that it already meets the analyzer’s correctness or speed requirements.

The incremental part is maintaining derived relations as edited method facts change, instead of evaluating all relations afresh for every edit. The proposal calls for handling differences in the input facts and their consequences. They are analysis inputs obtained from the method body after an edit, considered in relation to the inputs from before it. What matters for its meaning is that a method-body edit can remove some input facts and introduce others, and the maintained relations must respond to both.

They represent different information that can influence the findings. Points-to information concerns possible heap objects and aliasing; virtual-call information concerns possible call targets; taint information concerns propagation relevant to findings. A change to an earlier relation can alter what the later analysis must consider, so maintaining only previously derived taint facts would not necessarily expose every consequence of a changed alias or call target.

The proposal permits interdependent consequences rather than prescribing a single, one-way sequence. For example, changed points-to information may affect a possible virtual target, and a changed target may affect taint propagation across a call. The actual dependencies would have to be represented by the analysis. The proposal does not supply a complete rule set or assert that every change follows that illustrative chain.

It modifies the maintained points-to, virtual-call, and taint relations. Explain delete/rederive in ordinary terms.

When an edited method removes an input that supported a derived fact, the maintenance process must reconsider that fact and consequences that depended on it. Deletion removes conclusions that may no longer hold; rederivation checks whether those conclusions still follow from other remaining support. The paired operations avoid treating removal of one support as proof that a conclusion has no support at all.

Because method-body edits can remove as well as add inputs. An additions-only update could leave points-to relationships, virtual targets, or taint facts whose support no longer exists. Because the target is new, an update cannot depend solely on revisiting taint facts that already existed for that target at the call. The new virtual-call fact must be capable of initiating the relevant derivations.

I want to propose using versioned context-sensitive summaries and demand-driven sink slices for the incremental Java taint analyzer, invalidating callers and shared-heap readers when aliasing or virtual dispatch changes.

That is a proposed way to organize incremental work, not a demonstrated result. Versioned summaries would distinguish context-sensitive information derived before and after relevant changes. Demand-driven sink slices would focus analysis on information relevant to sink findings. Invalidation of callers and shared-heap readers acknowledges that alias or dispatch changes can have consequences beyond the edited method.
What is a context-sensitive summary in this proposal?

At a conceptual level, it captures analysis information about method behavior while preserving the calling-context distinctions relevant to taint results. The proposal does not specify a summary format, how contexts are identified, or what individual facts a summary contains.
What does versioning add to those summaries?

Versioning lets the analysis distinguish a summary associated with one state of the program from information that may need reconsideration after an edit. It provides a way to ask whether a summary is still applicable when dependencies change. The proposal does not prescribe version numbers, storage rules, or a particular test for applicability.
Does a new version mean every summary in the program must be rebuilt?

No such blanket rule is stated. The proposal couples versioned summaries with invalidation of callers and shared-heap readers on alias or dispatch changes. It aims to identify consequences of changes rather than assume that all summaries always require rebuilding. It does not, however, guarantee that an edit will affect only a small number of summaries.
And what is a demand-driven sink slice?

It is an analysis slice organized around what can matter to a sink finding. ‘Demand-driven’ means the relevant questions about taint are pursued from those finding-related demands rather than assuming every possible analysis fact must be reconsidered for every edit. The proposal leaves the representation of slices and the mechanics of demand propagation unspecified.
Is a sink slice just a list of findings already reported?

It cannot be understood only that way if it is to support exact updates. An edit can introduce an alias or virtual target that creates a path to a sink where no finding existed before. A slice restricted to the support of existing findings could miss that new path. The proposal does not specify how demands discover new paths, so that remains an important correctness question rather than a solved feature.
Why specifically invalidate callers on a dispatch change?

Changing the possible targets of a virtual call can change the behavior that contributes to its caller’s taint analysis. A caller relying on a context-sensitive summary may then need reconsideration, and effects may continue through further callers. The proposal names caller invalidation to account for that interprocedural dependency; it does not specify how far propagation goes in any particular case.
Could an alias change also make a caller’s summary inapplicable?

Potentially. A changed alias relationship can alter taint behavior through heap accesses and across calls. The proposal names invalidating callers on alias or dispatch changes because either category can affect information used beyond the edited method. Whether a particular caller actually changes would depend on its dependencies, which are not enumerated here.
Why add shared-heap readers to the invalidation targets?

A change to what may alias can alter which reads may observe effects through shared heap state. Such a reader might occur in a different method or context from the edit, even if it is not captured by considering only immediate callers. Including shared-heap readers makes those possible cross-context consequences part of the proposed invalidation scope.
Does ‘shared-heap readers’ mean every method that ever reads a field?

The proposal does not define it that broadly. It identifies readers of shared heap state as an invalidation concern when alias or dispatch changes affect their relevant information. It does not prescribe an indiscriminate invalidation of every field-reading method, nor specify the dependency test for selecting readers.
Is a dispatch change necessarily a change to a heap read?

No. Alias and dispatch changes are distinct categories. Either can have consequences for callers or shared-heap readers depending on the program. The proposal does not claim that every dispatch change affects heap state or that every alias change changes virtual-call targets.
How would a versioned summary and a sink slice relate to one another?

Conceptually, a sink-driven demand could use a context-sensitive method summary, while version information could help determine whether that summary remains applicable after a relevant change. If alias or dispatch information on which it depends has changed, the analysis would need to reconsider its use and any affected findings. This explains their intended roles together, not a specified cache protocol or evaluation order.
Can the analyzer simply accept a summary with the latest version number?

A version label alone would not establish that a summary accounts for every relevant alias, dispatch, or shared-heap dependency. The central question is whether the summary is valid for the edited program and the context in which it is used. The proposal names versioning but does not supply an adequacy rule for that check.
What about summaries for contexts that appear only because a new virtual target became possible?

That is an important addition case. A newly possible target may require considering method behavior in a context that was not previously relevant at that call. An incremental scheme cannot discover all such consequences solely by invalidating summaries already used there. The proposed demand and invalidation machinery would have to make the new possibility visible; the proposal does not yet demonstrate how.
If the sink-driven work is narrow, can we assume every untouched context is unaffected?

No. Leaving a context untouched is justified only if changes to aliasing, virtual targets, and shared heap state cannot change its contribution to the findings. A narrow slice is useful only if it still includes every relevant path, including paths created by an edit. The proposal gives an approach to investigate, not a proof that its slices always establish that boundary.
Does invalidation require deleting a finding outright?

Not necessarily. Invalidation means the existing basis for a summary or finding needs reconsideration. The final finding may remain supported by another path, disappear, or be joined by a newly justified finding. The proposal does not specify the reanalysis procedure used to determine which result holds.
Could a shared-heap reader be affected even when it is not a caller of the edited method?

Conceptually, yes. Shared heap state can connect computations across methods and contexts without a direct caller relationship to the edited method. That is why the proposal names shared-heap readers separately from callers. It does not identify any particular program or reader that exhibits this behavior.
Is the proposal limited to method-body edits?

The analyzer’s stated evaluation target concerns a fixed suite of 100 method-body edits, and this proposal is being considered for incremental updates when edits change aliasing or dispatch. It does not specify behavior for every possible kind of program change outside that setting.
What correctness standard would this approach still have to satisfy?

For Java without reflection or native calls, the incremental taint findings must equal those of sound, context-sensitive whole-program recomputation. Versioning, slicing, and invalidation cannot weaken that to approximate findings or a no-omissions-only check: additional findings would also be a mismatch.
Does context sensitivity apply only to summaries, or also to the findings comparison?

The proposal explicitly calls the summaries context-sensitive. Independently, the correctness reference is sound, context-sensitive whole-program recomputation. The proposal does not specify a context abstraction or prove that the summaries reproduce that reference’s distinctions.
Could the approach produce exact findings but still fail the overall performance goal?

Yes. Exact findings and performance are separate requirements. The goal is at least a 3× median speedup over full recomputation on the fixed suite of 100 method-body edits. Demand-driven work might be intended to reduce recomputation, but the proposal supplies no timing measurement or assurance that the median threshold will be met.
Could it be fast yet miss a sink introduced by a new alias?

That is a possible failure mode, not a reported outcome. If a new alias creates a relevant path and the update’s demands or invalidation do not reach it, the findings could differ from whole-program recomputation despite a fast update. The exact-findings requirement rules out treating speed as compensation for such a miss.
Does this proposal select a concrete slicing algorithm or a way to store versions?

No. It states the components to use—versioned context-sensitive summaries, demand-driven sink slices, and invalidation of callers and shared-heap readers on alias or dispatch changes—without specifying algorithms, data structures, dependency keys, or implementation details.
Should I say this approach has already achieved the ≥3× median speedup?

No. This is a proposal. Its wording gives neither a completed evaluation nor a performance result for the proposed combination. The ≥3× median speedup over full recomputation on the fixed 100-method-body-edit suite remains a target to assess.
How would you state the proposal and its unresolved obligation concisely?

Propose versioned context-sensitive summaries and demand-driven sink slices, invalidating callers and shared-heap readers when aliasing or virtual dispatch changes. The approach would still need to show that it discovers all changed sink findings—including newly possible paths—and matches sound, context-sensitive whole-program recomputation for Java without reflection or native calls, while meeting the ≥3× median speedup target on the fixed suite of 100 method-body edits.
How can demand-driven slices discover newly reachable sinks when an edit creates alias or dispatch edges outside the cached slices?

That is the unresolved discovery problem for the proposed approach. A cached slice reflects dependencies known when it was constructed. If an edit introduces an alias or possible virtual-call target outside that slice, a new path to a sink may appear without any existing finding—or cached dependency within the slice—to signal it. The update needs some way to make the new edge relevant to sink demands and extend or reconsider the appropriate slices; the proposal does not yet specify how.
Why can't we simply recheck the facts already in each cached sink slice?

Rechecking existing slice facts can assess paths the slice already represents. It may not discover a path whose connecting alias or dispatch edge did not previously exist within it. The challenge is identifying when a change outside a cached slice should expand the slice, without assuming the old slice is a complete description of all paths the edited program could have.
Does ‘newly reachable sink’ mean the program gained a new sink statement?

Not necessarily. A sink may already exist in the program but become reachable by a relevant taint path only after the edit. The question concerns that newly possible connection, not a requirement that the edit introduce a new sink statement.

Conceptually, suppose the cached analysis found no relevant connection between a tainted heap write and a read that can ultimately influence a sink. An edit makes their references potentially alias. The read can now matter to the sink demand, even though the alias edge connecting them was absent when the slice was cached. Simply reusing the old slice could overlook the new path. This is an illustration of the question, not a reported test case.
And what does a new dispatch edge change?

It can add a possible method target at a virtual call. Behavior through that target may connect taint to a sink that the cached slice did not previously include. The update must recognize that the newly possible target may enlarge the relevant interprocedural path, rather than only reconsidering targets already recorded in the slice.
If we invalidate callers on a dispatch change, doesn't that automatically find the sink?

Not automatically. Caller invalidation identifies analysis information that may need reconsideration, but the question is whether reconsideration can discover paths involving a target or dependency absent from the cached sink slice. The approach would need a way to connect the changed dispatch edge to the appropriate demands and follow any newly relevant consequences. The proposal does not establish that caller invalidation alone does so.
Would invalidating shared-heap readers settle the alias case instead?

It addresses an important kind of consequence: a changed alias can make a reader of shared heap state relevant across methods or contexts. But the discovery question remains whether the update can identify the appropriate readers and connect their new consequences to sink demands, including when those connections lie outside cached slices. Merely naming shared-heap readers as invalidation targets does not define that selection or propagation.
What does ‘outside cached slices’ imply about versioned summaries?

A version can help distinguish information that may need reconsideration, but a version label alone cannot expose a newly formed path to a sink. If a summary depends on changed alias or dispatch possibilities, the update must determine where the change matters, including potentially new uses of a summary. The question does not specify a versioning rule that solves that discovery problem.
Could we decide a slice is unaffected whenever none of its stored facts changed?

That would be unsafe as a general inference from the question. A new edge outside the stored slice may create a path into it or make a previously irrelevant method or heap access relevant to its sink. Establishing that a slice is unaffected requires accounting for potential new dependencies, not merely checking whether its existing entries were modified.
Is the issue just removing stale findings from old slices?

No. Retraction is important when support disappears, but this question focuses on additions that can create newly reachable sinks. If no prior finding exists along the new path, tracing only existing finding provenance would not reveal it. The update has to discover the newly relevant path as well as reconsider old ones when appropriate.
Does demand-driven mean we have to analyze every sink again after each edit?

Not by definition. Demand-driven analysis focuses work on what could matter to sink findings. The difficulty is defining a selective discovery boundary that still catches sinks made reachable by new alias or dispatch edges. The question neither prescribes a full rescan of all sinks nor establishes that a smaller update is always possible.
Suppose a changed edge is several method calls away from a sink. Can it be ignored because it isn't adjacent to the slice?

No. If its consequences can propagate through calls or shared heap state to alter a sink finding, distance from the cached slice does not make it irrelevant. A satisfactory answer would explain how those indirect interprocedural connections are discovered, while allowing genuinely unrelated contexts and slices to remain untouched.
What would an answer need to establish about slices that are left cached and unchanged?

It would need to justify that no newly created alias or dispatch dependency can change their sink-relevant results. In other words, the mechanism must explain both how it finds slices to expand and why the slices it leaves alone cannot acquire a new finding from the edit. Failure to find a connection through the current cache is not, by itself, such a justification.
If the new edge is detected, does that alone establish complete findings?

No. Detecting an edge is only the beginning. Its consequences might change virtual targets, heap-taint relationships, summaries, and ultimately sink findings across contexts. The update would need to follow every relevant dependency and reach any newly reachable sink, while avoiding unjustified findings. This question provides no specific traversal or update rule that guarantees that outcome.
What correctness comparison keeps us honest about newly reachable sinks?

For Java without reflection or native calls, incremental findings must equal those of sound, context-sensitive whole-program recomputation. A newly reachable sink finding present in recomputation but absent after a slice-based update would violate that equality. Extra findings would also be a mismatch; checking only that existing findings were preserved would be insufficient.
Does a successful finding comparison on some edits prove that cached slices can never miss a new path?

No. A comparison can establish equality for the evaluated edits, but the general question asks how discovery works whenever an edit adds an alias or dispatch edge outside a cached slice. Establishing that broader behavior requires an account of the dependency and invalidation mechanism, not only observations on a finite collection of edits.
Could scanning the whole program answer the correctness part of the question?

Whole-program recomputation supplies the reference findings, but using it after every edit would not answer the selective-incrementality part of the question. The goal also calls for at least a 3× median speedup over full recomputation on a fixed suite of 100 method-body edits. So checking only the version of an existing slice would not necessarily suffice?

Does ‘newly reachable sink’ require the edit to create a sink statement?

What if the first new edge leads through several calls and a heap access before reaching a sink?

Would a frontier have to contain every possible future taint path in advance?

We would need to account for whether changed call-site or heap-field reachability could connect to that sink demand, including through new paths absent from the cached slice. Does the hypothesis tell us which indexes or subscriptions find those connections?

What would count against the hypothesis in a findings comparison?

A whole-program finding at a newly reachable sink that the frontier-based update misses would contradict the predicted discovery. Any additional or other missing finding would contradict exact parity as well. This describes how to interpret a comparison; it does not report that one has been run.
